:::

This chapter is a fast tour of methods every analytics practitioner should recognise, even though each one could fill a deep dive of its own. The goal is not mastery in one sitting. It is vocabulary, intuition, and a working mental hook for where each method belongs.

Each family gets a short section here and one working R snippet further down, so the names click into the concrete code they map to. Two of them also get a figure you can work by hand. The curve above is the first: what you believe about a rate before you have seen anything, which the second section goes on to update.

## Tests without a distribution

When you don't know the underlying distribution, or can't assume one, there are three go-to nonparametric tests.

| Test | Data | Question |
|---|---|---|
| **McNemar's test** | Paired binary outcomes | Do two treatments differ? |
| **Wilcoxon signed-rank** | Paired or one-sample continuous | Is the median different? |
| **Mann-Whitney U** | Two independent samples | Are the distributions different? |

Take McNemar's. Two antibiotics are tested against the same 50 bacterial strains, and for each strain you record whether A worked and whether B worked. The test ignores the strains where the two agree and looks only at the disagreement cells. If one treatment dominates the disagreements, the p-value is small.

Picking the right test comes down to three questions. How many samples do you have? If two, are they paired or unpaired? And what are you asking about: a mean, a median, a success count? That is 80% of the decision. [Paired versus unpaired: Wilcoxon has both forms. In R they are the same function, `wilcox.test()`, with `paired = TRUE` for matched pairs and `paired = FALSE` for the Mann-Whitney version. Pick by whether the data come in matched pairs.]{.side}

## Updating a belief

Bayesian modelling answers one question: given what you believed before and what you have just seen, what should you believe now? The rule is

$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)}{P(B)}$$

The classic example is a medical test that is 98% sensitive, has an 8% false positive rate, and looks for a disease with 1% prevalence. After a positive result your chance of having the disease is still only about 11%. The healthy population is so much larger that it produces roughly eight times more false positives than the sick population produces true positives. [Base rate fallacy: even a 98% sensitive test on a 1% prevalence disease gives only about an 11% posterior probability of disease after a positive result.]{.side}

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="bayes-figure" data-step="1" data-steps="1:ten outcomes|2:observe more" data-caption="Fig. 2 · the same belief after the outcomes arrive, recomputed in your browser · made-up outcomes"}
:::

The figure does the same arithmetic with a whole curve in place of a single number. The prior is what you believed about a success rate before the data; the posterior is what you believe after. It lands between the prior and the observed rate, and each press of the button moves it further toward the data and makes it narrower. Slide the prior strength up and the same outcomes move it less.

That pull back toward the prior is called shrinkage, and empirical Bayes is where you meet it in practice. In NCAA basketball, model an observed margin as home-court advantage plus the true difference between the teams plus noise, with a home-court advantage of 4 points, a standard deviation of 11 points for game-to-game noise and 6 points for true team-strength differences. A team wins at home by 20. The model attributes about 4 of those points to home court, fewer than 4 to actual talent, and the rest to noise, so a 20-point home win is less than a 50% predictor of the same team winning on the road. Shrinkage is not intuitive: an extreme observed margin usually means noise, not a talent gap. Reach for it when you have lots of general data and little specific data.

## Communities in a graph

Given a network, which nodes belong together? The Louvain algorithm answers by maximising **modularity**, a measure of how much more tightly nodes are connected within a community than you would expect by random chance.

Each round works the same way. Start with every node in its own community. Move each node to whichever neighbouring community best increases modularity, and repeat until nothing moves. Then collapse each community into a super-node and go back to moving nodes.

The R below hand-computes modularity for a tiny six-node graph: two triangles joined by a single edge. Splitting it into the two triangles scores higher than putting every node in its own community or all six in one. That is the structural insight Louvain would climb to automatically. For real use, `igraph::cluster_louvain()` does the whole thing.

## Neural networks and language

A neural network is the tool for pattern recognition where the rules can't be written down. The `nnet` package ships with R, and a network with one hidden layer of five neurons, four input features and three output classes learns to classify the species in `iris` from 120 scaled training rows. The interesting thing is not the accuracy. It is how few lines it takes. Training is fast; making a network generalise to a new problem, with a different data distribution or a different task, is the hard part.

Natural language processing works on unstructured language data, and one small example shows why context matters. "I blew my nose", "I blew my chance" and "I blew my horn" share one syntax and use three different senses of "blew", and the last sentence alone has two different meanings. Modern NLP models handle this with context embeddings.

Even so, the simplest step is a useful starting point. Tokenise the sentence into words, lowercase them, strip the punctuation, and count. That frequency table is the base for bag-of-words models and the front end of every classical NLP pipeline. Modern transformers do much more, but they still start here. In R the tools are `tm`, `quanteda` or transformers.

## Opponents who react

Game theory is for decisions where the other side responds to what you do. Two gas stations sit on the same corner, each choosing a price of \$2.50 or \$2.00. Fuel costs them \$1.00 a gallon and total demand is 1,000 gallons. When the prices tie they split the demand; when they differ, the cheaper station captures everything.

Enumerate the payoff matrix and read it from your own side.

| Your profit | Other charges \$2.00 | Other charges \$2.50 |
|---|---|---|
| **You charge \$2.00** | \$500 | \$1000 |
| **You charge \$2.50** | \$0 | \$750 |

If the other station charges \$2.50, your best move is \$2.00 (\$1000 against \$750). If it charges \$2.00, your best move is still \$2.00 (\$500 against \$0). So two rational actors both land on \$2.00, which is worse for each of them than both charging \$2.50. That is the classic prisoner's dilemma. [Game-theoretic equilibria are not always cooperative. The prisoner's dilemma equilibrium is worse for everyone than the cooperative outcome.]{.side}

Now raise the cost to \$1.75. At the higher price each station earns \$0.75 on 500 gallons, which is \$375; at the lower price each earns \$0.25 on 500 gallons, which is \$125. The higher price now pays better for both players and the incentive to defect is gone. Economics, not morals, drive the equilibrium.

## Time until an event

Survival models predict the probability that an event happens before time $t$, as a function of covariates. Cox's proportional hazards model writes the hazard as

$$h(t \mid x) = h_0(t) \cdot \exp\left( \sum_j \beta_j x_j \right)$$

where $h_0(t)$ is the baseline hazard and each $\exp(\beta_j x_j)$ is a multiplicative factor on it. Fitted to the `lung` dataset from the `survival` package (the NCCTG lung cancer study), the `exp(coef)` column of the output is the hazard ratio. Above 1 it increases the hazard, meaning shorter survival; below 1 it decreases it. There `sex = 2`, female, has a hazard ratio below 1: the women in this dataset survived longer.

The defining feature of survival analysis is **censored data**. A patient still alive when the study ends has a right-censored survival time. Cox proportional hazards and the Kaplan-Meier curve both handle this naturally, and on a Kaplan-Meier plot the vertical ticks are the censored observations. Naive regression on survival time does not handle it. [Censoring: never run plain regression on survival data. It discards the information from the subjects who are still alive.]{.side}

## Correcting errors in rounds

Gradient boosting builds a strong learner by adding weak learners that each fit the residual errors of the current ensemble. Start with a simple baseline $F_0(x)$; the mean works fine. Compute the negative gradient of the loss at each training point, which for squared error is just the residuals. Fit a small learner $h_k(x)$ to those residuals, and update

$$F_{k+1}(x) = F_k(x) + \gamma \cdot h_k(x)$$

Then repeat.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="boost-figure" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 3 · the first small tree, fitted to what the mean leaves over · made-up data"}
:::

In the figure the small learner is a stump, a tree with one split, and the step size $\gamma$ is one half. The thin line is the stump fitted to the residuals; the heavy line is the model after half of it has been added. The step size can also be chosen analytically. In a hand-worked toy example with four data points, one full boosting iteration takes the squared error from 2.0 to 0.04 with an optimal step size $\gamma^* = 0.56$. When $h$ fits the residuals perfectly, $\gamma^* = 1$ and the error drops to zero. With an imperfect fit, which is the realistic case, $\gamma^*$ is smaller and the error drops by less, but every iteration improves the prediction.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="boost-figure" data-step="2" data-steps="0:the mean|1:one tree|2:add trees" data-caption="Fig. 4 · boosting run live in your browser, with the error on points it never saw · made-up data"}
:::

Add trees and watch both errors. The classic shape of the training error is a fast drop and then a plateau. Stop too early and you underfit; go too long and you overfit. [Boosting overfits: training error monotonically decreases but test error eventually climbs. Use early stopping or cross-validation to pick the number of iterations.]{.side}

Reach for boosting on tabular prediction with complex interactions. In R the tools are `gbm` and `xgboost`. The example below fits 500 trees of depth 3 with a shrinkage of 0.05, which is `gbm`'s name for the step size, to a nonlinear regression problem.

## Run it yourself {.reference}

One working snippet per family, in the order of the tour. Open "The R" under any of them to see the code.

McNemar's test on two antibiotics tried against the same 50 strains.

```{r}
#| label: mcnemar

set.seed(99)
n_strains <- 50
A_works <- rbinom(n_strains, 1, 0.55)
B_works <- rbinom(n_strains, 1, 0.80)

# McNemar ignores both-agree cells, tests the disagreement
contingency <- table(A_works, B_works)
contingency

mcnemar.test(contingency, correct = FALSE)
```

The Wilcoxon signed-rank test for a paired comparison of medians.

```{r}
#| label: wilcoxon

set.seed(7)
before <- rnorm(30, mean = 100, sd = 12)
after  <- before - rnorm(30, mean = 4, sd = 6)   # slight improvement

wilcox.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)
```

The Mann-Whitney U test for two unpaired samples.

```{r}
#| label: mann-whitney

group_a <- rnorm(40, mean = 50, sd = 10)
group_b <- rnorm(40, mean = 55, sd = 10)

wilcox.test(group_a, group_b, paired = FALSE)
```

Bayes' rule on the medical test: 98% sensitive, 8% false positives, 1% prevalence.

```{r}
#| label: bayes-medical

sensitivity <- 0.98    # P(+ | disease)
fpr         <- 0.08    # P(+ | no disease)
prevalence  <- 0.01

p_positive <- sensitivity * prevalence + fpr * (1 - prevalence)
p_disease_given_positive <- sensitivity * prevalence / p_positive

cat("P(positive test) =", round(p_positive, 4), "\n")
cat("P(disease | positive) =",
    round(p_disease_given_positive, 4),
    "(only about 11%!)\n")
```

Empirical Bayes shrinkage on a 20-point home win in NCAA basketball.

```{r}
#| label: empirical-bayes

# Parameters from historical NCAA data
H <- 4        # home-court advantage (points)
sigma <- 11   # SD of random game noise
tau <- 6      # SD of true team-strength differences

observed_margin <- 20
# Observed = H + M + noise, so "signal" = observed - H = 16 on top of home court

# Shrinkage: posterior mean of M given observation
# M | X ~ Normal(posterior_mean, posterior_var)
x_minus_h <- observed_margin - H
posterior_var  <- 1 / (1 / tau^2 + 1 / sigma^2)
posterior_mean <- posterior_var * (x_minus_h / sigma^2)

cat("Observed margin:             ", observed_margin, "\n")
cat("  - home-court component:    ", H, "\n")
cat("  - posterior mean of M:     ", round(posterior_mean, 2), "\n")
cat("  - attributed to randomness:",
    round(observed_margin - H - posterior_mean, 2), "\n")
cat("P(home team is truly better) =",
    round(1 - pnorm(0, posterior_mean, sqrt(posterior_var)), 3), "\n")
```

Modularity, computed by hand, for two triangles joined by one edge.

```{r}
#| label: modularity

# Adjacency matrix for two triangles connected by a single edge
A <- matrix(0, 6, 6)
# Triangle 1: nodes 1, 2, 3
A[1, 2] <- 1; A[2, 1] <- 1
A[1, 3] <- 1; A[3, 1] <- 1
A[2, 3] <- 1; A[3, 2] <- 1
# Triangle 2: nodes 4, 5, 6
A[4, 5] <- 1; A[5, 4] <- 1
A[4, 6] <- 1; A[6, 4] <- 1
A[5, 6] <- 1; A[6, 5] <- 1
# Bridge: 3-4
A[3, 4] <- 1; A[4, 3] <- 1

# Node weights (degree)
w <- rowSums(A)
# Total edge weight (undirected: sum(A) counts each edge twice)
W <- sum(A) / 2

modularity <- function(A, communities, w, W) {
  Q <- 0
  for (i in seq_along(communities)) {
    for (j in seq_along(communities)) {
      if (communities[i] == communities[j]) {
        Q <- Q + (A[i, j] - w[i] * w[j] / (2 * W))
      }
    }
  }
  Q / (2 * W)
}

# Two-community split (the "right" answer)
comm_good <- c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2)
# Each-own community
comm_singleton <- 1:6
# One big community
comm_single <- rep(1, 6)

cat("Modularity (two communities):  ", round(modularity(A, comm_good, w, W), 3), "\n")
cat("Modularity (each own cluster): ", round(modularity(A, comm_singleton, w, W), 3), "\n")
cat("Modularity (all one cluster):  ", round(modularity(A, comm_single, w, W), 3), "\n")
```

A network with one hidden layer, trained on `iris` with `nnet`.

```{r}
#| label: nnet
#| message: false

suppressMessages(library(nnet))

set.seed(1)

# Scale features
iris_scaled <- iris
iris_scaled[, 1:4] <- scale(iris[, 1:4])

train_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(iris)), size = 120)
train <- iris_scaled[train_idx, ]
test  <- iris_scaled[-train_idx, ]

model_nn <- nnet(Species ~ ., data = train, size = 5, decay = 0.01,
                 maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)

pred <- predict(model_nn, newdata = test, type = "class")
acc <- mean(pred == test$Species)
cat("Test accuracy:", round(acc, 3), "\n")

table(predicted = pred, actual = test$Species)
```

The payoff matrix for the two gas stations.

```{r}
#| label: prisoners-dilemma

d <- 1000   # total demand in gallons

payoff <- function(p_self, p_other, cost = 1.00, d = 1000) {
  if (p_self < p_other) {
    d * (p_self - cost)
  } else if (p_self > p_other) {
    0
  } else {
    (d / 2) * (p_self - cost)
  }
}

price_grid <- c(2.00, 2.50)
pm <- outer(price_grid, price_grid,
            Vectorize(function(a, b) payoff(a, b)))
rownames(pm) <- paste0("Self_$", price_grid)
colnames(pm) <- paste0("Other_$", price_grid)
pm
```

Tokenising a sentence and counting the words.

```{r}
#| label: nlp-toy

sentence <- "I blew my horn and then I blew my chance."
tokens <- strsplit(sentence, "\\s+")[[1]]
tokens

# Frequency table (the base for bag-of-words models)
token_clean <- gsub("[[:punct:]]", "", tolower(tokens))
table(token_clean)
```

A Cox proportional hazards model on the `lung` data, where `status == 2` means death.

```{r}
#| label: survival
#| message: false

suppressMessages(library(survival))

head(lung[, c("time", "status", "age", "sex", "ph.ecog")])

# Cox PH: status == 2 means death
fit_cox <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, data = lung)
summary(fit_cox)$coefficients
```

Kaplan-Meier survival curves for the same patients, by sex.

```{r}
#| label: plot-km
#| fig-cap: "Kaplan-Meier survival curves by sex. The vertical ticks are *censored* observations — patients still alive when the study ended."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

km_fit <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)

plot(km_fit, col = c("#1f4e79", "#d62828"), lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Days", ylab = "Survival probability",
     main = "Lung-cancer survival by sex")
legend("topright",
       legend = c("Male (sex=1)", "Female (sex=2)"),
       col = c("#1f4e79", "#d62828"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

Gradient boosting with `gbm` on a nonlinear regression problem.

```{r}
#| label: gbm
#| message: false
#| warning: false

suppressMessages(library(gbm))

set.seed(1)

n <- 500
x1 <- runif(n, -3, 3)
x2 <- runif(n, -3, 3)
y  <- sin(x1) + 0.5 * x2^2 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)

train_idx <- 1:400
train <- data.frame(x1, x2, y)[train_idx, ]
test  <- data.frame(x1, x2, y)[-train_idx, ]

fit_gbm <- gbm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = train,
               distribution = "gaussian",
               n.trees = 500, interaction.depth = 3,
               shrinkage = 0.05, verbose = FALSE)

pred <- predict(fit_gbm, newdata = test, n.trees = 500)
rmse <- sqrt(mean((test$y - pred)^2))
cat("Test RMSE:", round(rmse, 3), "\n")
```

The training error of that model at every boosting iteration.

```{r}
#| label: plot-gbm
#| fig-cap: "Training error as a function of number of boosting iterations. Classic shape: error drops fast, then plateaus. Stop too early and you underfit; go too long and you overfit."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

plot(fit_gbm$train.error, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#2d6a4f",
     xlab = "Boosting iteration", ylab = "Training error",
     main = "Boosting error vs iteration count")
grid()
```

The optimal step size $\gamma$ for one boosting step, worked out on four points.

```{r}
#| label: gbm-gamma

# Four points: F_0 predictions and residuals
y_true   <- c( 4,  5,  3,  1)
F_0_pred <- c(3.5, 5.5, 2.0, 1.5)   # base model predictions
residuals <- y_true - F_0_pred
residuals

# Imagine H_0 perfectly fits the residuals (it usually won't)
H_0_pred <- residuals

# Find optimal step size gamma for F_1 = F_0 + gamma * H_0
# Loss = sum((y - (F_0 + gamma * H_0))^2)
# dLoss/dgamma = -2 * sum(H_0 * (y - F_0 - gamma * H_0)) = 0
# => gamma = sum(H_0 * (y - F_0)) / sum(H_0^2)
gamma_star <- sum(H_0_pred * (y_true - F_0_pred)) / sum(H_0_pred^2)
cat("Optimal gamma:", round(gamma_star, 4), "\n")

F_1_pred <- F_0_pred + gamma_star * H_0_pred
sse_before <- sum((y_true - F_0_pred)^2)
sse_after  <- sum((y_true - F_1_pred)^2)

cat("SSE before boosting step:", round(sse_before, 4), "\n")
cat("SSE after  boosting step:", round(sse_after,  4), "\n")
```

## On one page {.reference}

| Topic | When to use | Key R tool |
|---|---|---|
| McNemar | Two paired binary outcomes | `mcnemar.test()` |
| Wilcoxon | Medians (paired or one-sample) | `wilcox.test(paired = TRUE)` |
| Mann-Whitney | Two independent distributions | `wilcox.test()` |
| Empirical Bayes | Lots of general data + little specific data | compute shrinkage by hand |
| Louvain | Find communities in a graph | `igraph::cluster_louvain()` (not shown — install for real use) |
| Neural network | Pattern recognition where rules aren't expressible | `nnet::nnet()` |
| Game theory | Agents who react to your decisions | enumerate payoff matrix |
| NLP | Unstructured language data | `tm` / `quanteda` / transformers |
| Cox PH | Time-to-event with covariates | `survival::coxph()` |
| Gradient boosting | Tabular prediction with complex interactions | `gbm` / `xgboost` |

## Check yourself {.reference}

Six common pitfalls. Before moving on, make sure you can explain each one without scrolling up:

1. **Base rate fallacy.** Even a 98% sensitive test on a 1% prevalence disease gives only ~11% posterior probability of disease after a positive result.
2. **Shrinkage is not intuitive.** Extreme observed margins usually mean noise, not talent gaps.
3. **Paired vs unpaired.** Wilcoxon has both forms — pick based on whether the data comes in matched pairs.
4. **Censoring.** Never run plain regression on survival data — it discards the information from still-alive subjects.
5. **Boosting overfits.** Training error monotonically decreases but test error eventually climbs. Use early stopping or CV to pick number of iterations.
6. **Game-theoretic equilibria are not always cooperative.** The prisoner's dilemma equilibrium is worse for everyone than the cooperative outcome.
